text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Scory v. Krannitz,

2011 BCSC 936

Date:
20110712

Docket:
S21632

Registry: Chilliwack

Between:

Robin
Scory

Plaintiff

And

Sian
Krannitz, Jack DeWitte and

Glen Valley Watershed Society

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Joyce

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Defendant DeWitte:

R.S.
Brearley

The Plaintiff appearing In Person:

Place and Date of Hearing:

Chilliwack,
B.C.

March
24, 2011

Place and Date of Judgment:

Chilliwack,
B.C.

July
12, 2011

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The plaintiff is an owner of lands situated
within the Township of Langley (the “Township”) located in the agricultural
land reserve. He wishes to obtain a permit from the Township to deposit fill on
his lands for farming and agricultural purposes.

[
2
]

The defendants are opposed to the proposal. The
defendant Krannitz owns property adjacent to Mr. Scory’s property and is a
member of the Glen Valley Watershed Society, whose mission is to protect and
enhance the ecological integrity of local watersheds in the Langley area. The
defendant DeWitte, owns and occupies lands that are located about 250 metres to
the north of the plaintiff’s lands.

[
3
]

In or about November 2009, the plaintiff
submitted a Notice of Intent to Deposit Soil for agricultural purposes to the
Township. The plaintiff alleges that the defendants began a public campaign
designed to oppose his application. There have been appearances before the
Township’s Council at which the parties have made representations for and
against the proposal.

[
4
]

The plaintiff has brought this action against
the defendant alleging several causes of actions arising out of the defendants’
statements and actions. The defendant DeWitte seeks an order dismissing the
claim against him.

THE LEGAL TEST

[
5
]

The defendant DeWitte, applies under Rules
9-5(1)(a) and (b) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg. 168/2009,
which provide:

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case
may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious.

The test for
determining whether an action may be struck for disclosing no reasonable claim
under Rule 9-5(1)(a) is as set out in
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990]
S.C.J. No. 93, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, where, speaking of the predecessor
rule, the Court said at para. 33:

33
... [A]ssuming the facts as stated in the statement of claim
can be proved, is it ‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff’s statement of
claim discloses no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a
chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be
‘driven from the judgment seat’.

[
6
]

A pleading is unnecessary or vexatious pursuant
to Rule 9-5(1)(b) if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of
action or does not advance any claim known in law [
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.)
at para.
47]
.

[
7
]

Whether the application is brought under Rule
9-5(1)(a) or (b), the applicant must satisfy the court that it is “plain and
obvious that the pleading offends the subrule in question [
Xu v. Foo

(2006),
2006 BCCA 525 (CanLII)
, 62 B.C.L.R. (4th) 132 (C.A.) at para.
54]
.

THE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST MR. DEWITTE

[
8
]

The claim against Mr. DeWitte is based on
statements allegedly made by him at the April 26, 2010 Township of Langley
Council Meeting. The relevant pleadings are found in paras. 55-68 of the Notice
of Civil Claim, which read as follows:

55.       Jack DeWitte resides at 7790-264th
St in the Township of Langley.

56.       Jack DeWitte is not a farmer.

57.       The DeWitte residence is in the ALR and is 250 meters
north of the Scory farm.

58.       Jack DeWitte, on or about April 26,2010, publicly stated
at the Township of Langley(TOL) council meeting that in 2005-2006 his well had
been covered 2 feet of rocks and debris allegedly from a farm soil deposit
site, approximately 2 kilometers upstream from the DeWitte property.

59.       Jack DeWitte presented no evidence, no before and after
photos or any relevant documentation to support his statement.

60.       In 2005-2006, on or about the time of Jack DeWitte's
alleged well damage, the Langley area experienced a record rainfall, with heavy
rain falling for an unprecedented 29 out 30 days. All Lower Mainland streams
and creeks experienced major flooding and erosion at that time.

61.       Jack DeWitte did not present this fact to the TOL Mayor,
Council and public at the April 26, 2010 Township council meeting.

62.       Jack DeWitte has personal access to historical weather and
rainfall records.

63.       It is not physically possible for a farm to generate more
water, rocks and debris than naturally present in streambeds or stream banks.

64.       The farmer allegedly responsible for the rocks and debris
covering Jack DeWitte's well in 2005-2006, does not know Jack DeWitte, has
never been contacted by Jack DeWitte and was unaware of Jack Dewitte's
accusations.

65.       The farmer became aware of Jack DeWitte's allegations when
he saw an interview about Jack DeWitte's well allegations and a photo of Jack
DeWitte in the local newspaper, The Aldergrove Star. Jack DeWitte contacted The
Aldergrove Star to publicly make his allegations.

66.       Jack DeWitte offered no explanation why he did not report
his well damage to the alleged responsible farmer or to the TOL, 5 years ago
when the incident occurred.

67.       Jack DeWitte offered no explanation why he chose a public
forum, 5 years after the alleged incident to make his accusations.

68.       Jack DeWitte's
statements have caused damage and harm to the plaintiff and the plaintiff’s
farm development. Jack DeWitte's statements have caused the TOL Mayor and
Council, TOL residents and the public to associate farms and farm soil deposit
with damaging nearby water wells.

[
9
]

The plaintiff claims, against all defendants,
damages based on: loss of farming production; loss of revenue from soil
deposit; loss of ability to generate farm revenue; and violation of his rights
under sections 7 and 8 of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms, Part

I

of the

Constitution Act, 1982
,
being

Schedule B to
the
Canada Act 1982
(U.K.)
,
1982, c. 11. He also pleads in
aid of his claim the
Farm Practices Protection (Right to Farm) Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c.131 [
FPPA
].

POSSIBLE CAUSES OF ACTION

[
10
]

Mr. DeWitte identifies the following causes
of action that the plaintiff might suggest his pleadings, on a liberal reading,
support:

(a)       a breach of the
FPPA
;

(b)       breaches of
sections 7
and
8
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
;

(c)        a
claim in negligence;

(d)       a
claim in negligent misrepresentation;

(e)       a claim
in unlawful act conspiracy; and

(f)         a claim
for unlawful interference with economic interests;

(g)       defamation;
and

(h)        injurious falsehood.

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS

[
11
]

I will deal with the potential claims identified
above in the order in which the defendant dealt with them.

Defamation

[
12
]

To establish a claim in defamation the plaintiff
would have to establish three things:

(1)       that the impugned words were defamatory, in the sense that
they would tend to lower the plaintiff’s reputation in the eyes of a reasonable
person;

(2)       that
the words in fact referred to the plaintiff; and

(3)       that the words were published, meaning that they were
communicated to at least one person other than the plaintiff.

[See:
Grant v. Torstar Corp.
,
2009
SCC 61
, at para
28
.]

[
13
]

I agree with counsel for Mr. DeWitte that
to the extent the words spoken by Mr. DeWitte, as set out in para. 58 of
his pleading, refer to
anyone
, they refer to the farmer of the upstream
property referred to in paras. 64 and 65 of the pleading. There is no
suggestion that the plaintiff is the object of Mr. DeWitte’s words.

[
14
]

I also agree with Mr. DeWitte’s submission
that the plaintiff does not plead damage to his reputation and that the words
spoken do not tend to adversely affect anyone’s reputation.

Injurious Falsehood

[
15
]

The plaintiff submitted that the basis of his
claim against Mr. DeWitte is the tort of injurious falsehood.

[
16
]

In
Captain Developments Ltd. v. Nu-West Group
Ltd.
(1982),
1982 CanLII 1747 (ON HCJ)
, 37 O.R. (2d) 697 (Ont. H.C.), rev’d on other grounds (1984),
1983 CanLII 1886 (ON CA)
, 45
O.R. (2d) 213 (C.A.) Montgomery J. accepted the formulation of injurious
falsehood contained in Fleming’s,
The Law of Torts
, 5
th
ed.
(1977) at p. 697:

Injurious
falsehood... consists in the publication of false statements, whether oral or
in writing, concerning the plaintiff or his property, calculated to induce
others not to deal with him ... the falsehood must be communicated to a third
person ... falsity is not presumed but must be affirmatively established by the
plaintiff.

[
17
]

Mr. DeWitte submits that the statement
attributed to him in para. 58 was not made concerning him but was made
concerning the upstream farmer. The plaintiff submits that a person hearing
that statement in the context of a town meeting concerned with the plaintiff’s
application to deposit soil would conclude that Mr. DeWitte was, by
necessary implication, making a false statement that if the plaintiff were
permitted to deposit soil, wells would be adversely affected and that the
statement was, therefore, made “concerning” the plaintiff.

[
18
]

In my view, that is an untenable argument which
gives far too broad a meaning to the phrase “concerning the plaintiff or his
property”. I am satisfied, on the authorities that the false statement must be related
to something done by the plaintiff or to some aspect of the plaintiff’s
property and that the statement alleged falls well short of meeting that
requirement.

[
19
]

I agree with Mr. DeWitte that the claim of
injurious falsehood is bound to fail.

Claim under the
Farm Practices Act

[
20
]

I accept Mr. DeWitte’s submission that the
Farm
Practices Act
does not grant positive right to farmers or give rise to a
cause of action. The
Act
establishes defences for farmers who are sued
by others. The plaintiff did not make any submissions in an effort to uphold this
purported cause of action.

Claim under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

[
21
]

Mr. DeWitte argues, and I agree, that there
are two reasons why a claim cannot be maintained on this footing. First, the
factual allegations said to give rise to the claim, which involve flying over
his property and photographing it, are made against the other defendants, not
Mr. DeWitte. Second, the
Charter
does not apply in litigation
between private citizens (
Dolphin Delivery Ltd. v. R.W.D.S.U., Local 580
,

1986 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573, 9 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273 at para.
40
).

Negligent Misrepresentation

[
22
]

The required elements for a successful claim
based on negligent misrepresentation were summarized in
Queen v. Cognos Inc.
,

1993 CanLII 146 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 87 at para.
33
:

33
(1) there must be a duty of care based on a "special
relationship" between the representor and the representee; (2) the
representation in question must be untrue, inaccurate, or misleading; (3) the
representor must have acted negligently in making said misrepresentation; (4)
the representee must have relied, in a reasonable manner, on said negligent
misrepresentation; and (5) the reliance must have been detrimental to the
representee in the sense that damages resulted.

[
23
]

The plaintiff does not allege that any representations
were made to him by Mr. DeWitte; the representations were made to others.
Further, there is no suggestion that he relied on any representations made by
Mr. DeWitte. In any event, the relationship between the plaintiff and
Mr. DeWitte is not one that, in my view, could possibly give rise to a
duty of care in that it cannot be said that in these circumstances Mr. DeWitte
could reasonable have foreseen that the plaintiff would rely on anything he
said or that reliance by the plaintiff would be reasonable. There is no
possibility, in my view, that the plaintiff could succeed on this ground.

Negligence

[
24
]

Mr. DeWitte submits that it is plain and
obvious that no duty of care was owed by him to the plaintiff in the
circumstances which could found an action in negligence.

[
25
]

The plaintiff’s claim is for pure economic
loss. I have not been provided with any case in which an individual
lobbying in his own interests has been held to owe a duty of care to an
individual with adverse interests for economic losses arising from those
lobbying efforts.

[
26
]

Mr. DeWitte says that The Supreme Court of
Canada has, to date, recognized five categories of negligence claims for pure
economic loss: negligent misrepresentation, negligent performance of a service,
defective products or buildings, relational economic loss, and independent
liability of statutory public authorities [
Martel Building Ltd. v. Canada
,

2000 SCC 60 (CanLII)
, [2000] 2 S.C.R. 860, at para
38]
.

[
27
]

As the plaintiff’s claim does not fit into any
of these recognized categories, an analysis must be undertaken in accordance
with
Cooper v. Hobart
, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 537,
2001 SCC 79
to determine
whether or not a duty of care should be found to exist in this case. This
analysis involves two questions: (1) Does the relationship between the
plaintiff and the defendant disclose sufficient foreseeability and proximity to
establish a
prima facie
duty of care; and (2) If so, are there any
residual policy considerations which ought to negate or limit that duty of
care? [See
Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board
,
2007 SCC 41 (CanLII)
, [2007]
S.C.J. No. 41 at para.
20
.]

[
28
]

The proximity test involves the question whether
the defendant was in a “close and direct relationship” with the plaintiff
making it just to impose on him a duty of care towards the plaintiff [
Fraser
v. Westminer Canada Ltd.
, [2003] N.S.J. No. 266 (C.A.),
2003 NSCA 76
[
Fraser
]
at para.
78]
.

[
29
]

At para. 79 of
Fraser
, Cromwell J.A.
(as he then was) said:

79

While there is no precise definition of what constitutes such a
close and direct relationship, the gist of the requirement is that there should
be "such close and direct relations that the act complained of directly
affects a person whom the person alleged to be bound to take care would know
would be directly affected by his careless act.":
Donoghue v. Stevenson
,

1932 CanLII 536 (FOREP)
, [1932] A.C. 562 (H.L.) at 581. In both
D'Amato v. Badger
,
1996 CanLII 166 (SCC)
, [1996] 2
S.C.R. 1071 at para.
49
and in McLachlin, J.'s judgment in
Norsk
[
Canadian
National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co.
,
1992 CanLII 105 (SCC)
, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 1021] at
paras. 48-53, a number of indicators of proximity are referred to. They
include the relationship between the parties, physical "propinquity"
(nearness in space), assumed or imposed obligations and the existence of a
close causal connection between the act and the harm suffered.

[
30
]

Mr. DeWitte says that the plaintiff has not
made express the duty he asserts was owed by Mr. DeWitte, but that
considering the nature of the allegations, the duty must be “something in the
nature of: a duty to take care in the representations that are made to elected
officials so that another citizen’s economic interests are not injured”.

[
31
]

Mr. DeWitte says that:

•

There is no plea of reliance.

•

No representations are alleged to have been made
to the plaintiff. The allegation is that representations were made to the
Township’s Council.

•

The relationship between Mr. DeWitte and
the plaintiff is adversarial in nature. Mr. DeWitte attended a Council
meeting to advocate on his own behalf and in his own interests. His efforts
were adverse to those who hold a contrary view.

[
32
]

Mr. DeWitte submits, and I agree, that the
plaintiff could not reasonably expect that those adverse to his interests would
act to take care of his interests. I agree with his submissions that “no credible
expectation links these two parties in a proximate relationship”.

[
33
]

I also agree with Mr. DeWitte’s submission
that no “close causal connection” could be proven between Mr. DeWitte’s
statement and the harm allegedly suffered by the plaintiff. The decision of the
Township to deny the permit, if that is its decision, is the cause of the
damage. The reasons for its decision will likely never be known.

[
34
]

I am of the view that no
prima facie
duty
of care should be recognized in these circumstances.

[
35
]

Even if a
prima facie
duty of care were
recognized, I am of the opinion that there are compelling policy reasons that
negate any such duty upon Mr. DeWitte in respect of the statements made at
the Township meeting. First, is the notion of indeterminate liability. All persons
who suffered economic injury as a result of a Council’s decision stemming from
a citizen’s advocacy would be able to assert a similar duty against the
advocate. The bounds of liability are immeasurable.

[
36
]

Second, such a duty would stifle public
participation in the democratic process. I agree with Mr. DeWitte
that members of the Township’s Council have an interest in receiving the views
of their constituents.

[
37
]

I am satisfied, therefore, that the plaintiff
has no chance of establishing liability on the basis of negligence.

Conspiracy

[
38
]

A conspiracy requires that parties act in
combination with each other. There is no allegation or suggestion that
Mr. DeWitte acted in combination with the other defendants or with other unnamed
co-conspirators. In my view, this claim must necessarily fail.

Unlawful Interference with Economic Interests

[
39
]

In
671122 Ontario Ltd. v. Sagaz Industries
Canada Inc.
,
1998 CanLII 14850 (ON CTGD)
, 40 O.R. (3d) 229, [1998] O.J. No. 2194, varied on other
grounds [2000] S.C.C.A. No. 141, aff’d [2001] S.C.J. No. 61,
2001 SCC
59
Cumming J. at para. 56, defined the elements of what he called the “emergent
tort” of unlawful interference with economic relations as:

(1) the existence of a valid business
relationship or business expectancy between the plaintiff and another party;
(2) knowledge by the defendant of that business relationship or expectancy; (3)
intentional interference which induces or causes a termination of the business
relationship or expectancy; (4)
the interference is by way of unlawful means
;
(5) the interference by the defendant must be the proximate cause of the
termination of the business relationship or expectancy; and (6) there is a
resultant loss to the plaintiff.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
40
]

Having concluded that there is no possibility
that the plaintiff can succeed in establishing any of the other alleged torts,
and there being no suggestion of any other way in which Mr. DeWitte acted
unlawfully, I conclude that it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot
succeed on this basis.

[
41
]

In summary, I am satisfied that it is plain and
obvious that the plaintiff’s claim against Mr. DeWitte cannot succeed. There
will, therefore, be an order dismissing the claim against them.

COSTS

[
42
]

Mr. Dewitte argues that the plaintiff’s
claim has no merit and is simply intended to intimidate Mr. DeWitte and
persons like him with similar interests from participating in public debate. He
argues that the action is damaging to the public at large, which depends on
free and open discussion as an integral component of its government.

[
43
]

Mr. DeWitte refers to
Fraser v. Saanich
(District),
[1999] B.C.J. No. 3100 (S.C.)
[
Fraser v. Saanich (District)
]
as authority for his submission that special costs are warranted. In that case,
the plaintiff applied to the District of Saanich for approval to redevelop a
nursing home and was denied approval. She commenced an action against the
District and a number of neighbourhood residents who signed a petition opposing
the proposed redevelopment, alleging negligence, conspiracy, bad faith, breach
of fiduciary duty and interference with contractual relations. The defendant
applied under what was then Rule 19(24)(a) to strike out the writ and statement
of claim as disclosing no reasonable claim.

[
44
]

The learned chambers judge held the claim was
without merit and was a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP)
that had been used to stifle the democratic activities of the defendants and
was deserving of censure by an award of special costs.

[
45
]

In my opinion, the same conclusion can be made
with respect to this case. The defendant DeWitte is, therefore, entitled to his
costs as special costs.

“B.M. Joyce J.”
